t: LONG BALL WATCH STARTS KEEPING SCORE - TRAINING DATA COLLECTION IS ON
x: The home-run list now grades itself. Every morning the system logs its full slate of predictions - all ~330 eligible hitters, every factor behind each number, and the sportsbook prices - not just the fifteen that make the board. Every night it checks the boxscores and records who actually went deep, who didn't, and who never played. That growing archive is the raw material for a REAL trained home-run model: today's version is honest arithmetic, but arithmetic can't learn which of its inputs matter most or how they interact - a trained model can, and it needs graded examples to learn from. This is the same playbook as the pitch-by-pitch bullpen archive: collect first, hypothesize later, and let every claim face graded results. The display doesn't change today. What changes is that from now on, every number the list publishes is on the record - and when there are enough graded days in the bank, the hand-built math has to beat what the data teaches, or it gets replaced by it.

t: BET WINDOW TIGHTENED TO 3-6% - THE DATA MOVED THE CAP
x: The play window was 3-8% since V2 launched, with the cap always described as humility, encoded. We regraded every tracked game by edge size at a finer grain, and the humility needed to move: 3-6% edges won 57.9% of 171 graded games and account for essentially all of the season's profit, while the 6-8% zone won just 47% of 100 and lost money - the 7-8% slice was the worst bucket on the whole curve at 42%. So the cap comes down from 8 to 6, effective today. What this means for you: slightly fewer plays, and the plays that survive come from exactly the zone that has been paying all season. The honest footnote: the 6-7% sliver graded mildly positive on its own, but 43 games is too thin to hang a rule on - if the curve says it earned its way back in a few hundred games from now, the window can move again. Same discipline as ever: the window is built on graded results, not on how confident the model feels.

t: LONG BALL WATCH - DAILY HOME RUN PROBABILITIES ON THE BOARD
x: New section on the board: the fifteen hitters most likely to go deep today, with the model's probability for each and real sportsbook prices next to it. The math is simple and fully inspectable: the hitter's season home-run rate (pulled toward league average so a hot week can't fake its way up the list), how he hits the opposing starter's throwing hand, that starter's own home-run tendency, the ballpark he's hitting in tonight, the wind when it's blowing out or in at an open-air park, and how many trips to the plate he usually gets. FAIR is the model's number expressed as American odds; DK/MGM/CZR are the books' actual 'to hit a home run' prices as they post them. Two honest caveats ship with it. One: even the best slugger alive only homers about one day in four - the numbers look low because home runs are genuinely rare, not because the model is shy. Two: this is a DISPLAY, not a betting product - no bet flags, no texts, no ledger, and gaps between FAIR and a book's price are entertainment until this list has a graded record. Same rule as everything else here: if it ever wants to become a play, it has to earn that on paper first.

t: BULLPEN AVAILABILITY TESTED - NOT ADOPTED. THE BULLPEN CHAPTER CLOSES
x: The last and best version of the bullpen idea: not how good the relievers are, but which arms are actually AVAILABLE tonight. Using our new pitch-by-pitch usage archive (every reliever's workload, every day, all season) we measured each team's bullpen burden over the previous two days, counted tired arms (20+ pitches yesterday or back-to-back outings), and counted rested top arms. Walk-forward across 556 games: nothing. Burden was an exact tie with the model alone; every other version was slightly worse. That completes the bullpen family - quality (tested), exposure (tested), availability (tested) - four trials, zero survivors. The market prices bullpens fine; our edge lives in the starter innings, which is exactly what the F5 paper experiment exists to isolate. The usage archive keeps growing nightly regardless: good data outlives the hypothesis that ordered it.

t: F5 SHADOW RULES TIGHTENED - LOCKS WITH LINEUPS, FINDS ITS OWN WINDOW
x: Three upgrades to the first-5 paper experiment. One: paper flags now lock at the exact moment the real play locks - the lineup-confirmed evaluation. A pre-lineup F5 flag that does not survive that evaluation drops off the site and never enters the ledger, same rule as real leans. Two: only lineup-confirmed paper bets count in the record. Three: instead of assuming the full-game 3-8% betting window transfers to a different market, the ledger now grades EVERY locked game by edge size - so the first-5 market can reveal its own best window from live data. When the sample is big enough, the window we use will be the one the data chose, not the one we inherited.

A subscriber-grade idea: do not just measure bullpen quality - measure how MUCH bullpen each team will need. We estimated every starter's expected innings from his last five starts (the hook), multiplied the leftover innings by recent bullpen ERA, and asked whether that burden gap predicts winners on top of the model. Walk-forward answer: it makes the model WORSE - 3 to 4 points of accuracy worse - and the hook estimate alone was worse still. That is now three bullpen-family ideas tested and three rejections, which matches everything else we know: our losses are decided in the starter innings, not the late ones. The deeper version (which specific reliever enters, how rested each arm is, platoon-driven hooks) stays on the candidate list but needs months of usage data we are now positioned to collect. Meanwhile the F5 shadow IS the answer to this insight from the other direction: instead of modeling the innings we cannot see, bet only the innings we can.

t: F5 SHADOW LAUNCHED - FIRST-5-INNINGS MODEL ON PAPER
x: The loss autopsy showed our losses die early: games decided in the starter innings, exactly where the model's features live. Follow-up test: scored against 683 live games, the model predicts the FIRST FIVE INNINGS winner at 57.7% vs 53.2% for full games. Starters own innings 1-5; every inning after that adds bullpen noise the model does not handicap. So we built a second head: same four features, retrained to predict the first-5 winner, and pointed it at real first-5 moneyline prices from four books. The catch that keeps this on paper: F5 markets are priced off the same starter stats we use and charge about a point more vig, so higher accuracy does not automatically mean profit. It now logs shadow bets every slate - no money, no texts - and the ledger is public in THE LEDGER below. Decision after 50+ paper flags. The de-vig experiment taught us why: its backtest said +8.6%, its live ledger said no. Everything earns its way in live or stays out.

t: LOSS AUTOPSY - NO HIDDEN FLAW FOUND
x: We put every graded loss under the microscope looking for what they share: price range, edge size, home/away, claimed confidence, starter quality, bullpen freshness, lineup strength, park, line movement. The honest headline: losses look almost exactly like wins. The model was NOT more confident on its losses (53.7% claimed vs 54.7% on wins), edges were the same size, and starter metrics were nearly identical - there is no cluster of games where the model was fooled in a diagnosable way. One suspect did emerge: losses skewed toward games where the OPPONENT'S bullpen had been fresher over the prior week. So we ran the full walk-forward trial - does 7-day bullpen ERA improve predictions on top of the model? Answer: no. Slightly worse, in fact. Week-old bullpen ERA is too noisy to carry signal; the cluster was small-sample coincidence. What survives: a smarter fatigue measure (actual pitches thrown, days of rest) is still on the candidate list, and home-side plays running cooler than road plays stays on the watch list. Every suspicion gets the same trial; this one came back clean.

Second feature idea of the day: weight pitcher stats toward recent starts (last-5 or decaying average) instead of full season. Tested on 649 games with true point-in-time data - only starts BEFORE each game counted. Result: pure recent-form was 2-3 points WORSE than season-to-date; blends were ties. Five starts of ERA is mostly luck - weighting toward it weights toward noise. The idea survives in better form: recent VELOCITY and swing-and-miss stabilize in a single game and can flag a declining arm long before ERA does. That version is on the candidate list with data collection underway. Every idea gets the same trial; most lose; the record is why.

A sharp outside suggestion: ERA describes the past; skill estimators like FIP and K-BB predict the future better. We ran the full walk-forward gauntlet on 3,454 out-of-sample games. Result: replacing our pitching feature with FIP or K-BB made the model 1.3-1.6 points WORSE; adding them alongside added nothing. Why: our pitching input was never raw ERA - it is capped to a plausible talent range and blended toward career numbers by sample size, which already removes most of the luck that skill estimators exist to remove. Every feature idea gets this same trial: beat the baseline out-of-sample or stay out of the model.

Player stats follow the PLAYER, not the team - a traded pitcher's ERA, sample size, and a traded hitter's platoon numbers all travel with him automatically. But the league's data feed reports traded players in per-team chunks, and the model could previously read only the newest chunk - meaning a deadline acquisition might have been judged on 3 innings with his new club instead of his full season. Fixed everywhere: the model now always uses full-season combined numbers regardless of how many uniforms a player has worn. Shipped before any post-deadline slate was played.

After a 1-7 stretch (-$600 over four days) we audited every play in the slump against the TRUE closing line, pulled from pre-pitch snapshots. All 8 plays beat the close, averaging +5.1% - the market moved toward our number after every single bet. The model's own probabilities expected ~4.4 wins from those 8 plays; getting 1 is a ~2% unlucky tail that any bettor eats a few times a season. Composition showed no pattern: losses spread across dogs and favorites, no team, no price band. Verdict: variance, not decay - no changes made. The tripwire that WOULD trigger changes: a slump arriving with negative closing-line value. This was the opposite. Running: 21-19, +$271, +6.8% ROI - inside the sustainable range we forecast when the record was running hot at +27%.

Two-part rule, built from a subscriber question about a thin-sample ace. (1) The starter on OUR side of a bet must have a real season sample (~50+ innings) - bets trusting our own thin data went 11-22, -$759. (2) Betting AGAINST a thin starter is allowed (16-13, +$269 historically) UNLESS his whiff rate says the stuff is elite - thin starters with real swing-and-miss win 55% of their games. Translation: we will fade an unproven call-up, but never a returning ace the market knows better than our career-stat blend does.

Complete rebuild. The old 18-feature XGBoost pipeline is retired after a teardown found six defects, including a lineup-swap bug that fed each team's offense into the model under the other team's name. V2 is a 4-feature calibrated logistic regression: simpler, better, fully auditable. Walk-forward accuracy 60.2% vs 58.7% for the old model across 3,187 out-of-sample games.

Park factor, home boost, bullpen nudge, and the 30-70 clamp are gone. Re-scoring 117 live games showed these layers flipped 28% of picks and lost most of the flips. The calibrated number is now used as-is.

The score-keeper was grading value-dog bets on the wrong team - when the flag was on the underdog, wins were recorded as losses. 13 bets corrected; season P&L swung over $1,200 in our favor. All graders now share one source of truth for which side carries the bet.
Locked-pick alerts now shop DraftKings, BetMGM, FanDuel, Caesars, Hard Rock, and Circa, ranking every price by payout and calling out the best number.

Alerts now translate model probability into fair American odds, and show an informational quarter-Kelly stake (capped 2% bankroll). Kelly stays informational until the model proves itself over 100 graded picks. If the Kelly line is missing, the price has moved and the value is gone - pass.

Backtest of a vig-free edge measure: 53% win / +8.6% ROI on 109 bets vs 48% / +0.5% for the current method. The true profit zone is a 3-6% de-vigged edge (62% win rate). Running in shadow mode - every slate logs both measures - before any switch.
Once a play is texted, it is frozen at the texted price. No later re-run can change its flag, side, or odds. The texted price is always the official play.
The odds feed returns multiple days of games; prices were keyed by team name and could mix tomorrow's lines into today's board. All price consumers now filter to the exact slate date.

Every graded game re-scored against the real line 10 minutes before its first pitch (545 games of historical snapshots). Honest result: raw picks beat the close only 53% of the time - but flagged plays beat it 96% of the time at +6.5% average. The market's final verdict almost never says our plays were wrong.
